articles.author: Jen Sherman
articles.content: The US has more big chains but in Australia produce is better quality – and bread doesn’t taste like cake I poked. I pulled. I looked in confusion at the head of garlic I was holding, wondering why the cloves weren’t coming apart. When I dug my nails in and finally broke out a clove, its skin was pierced and there were scratch marks in the flesh. It had only been a few weeks since I moved back to Australia from the US, after a 10-year stint in San Diego; only a few weeks since I cooked with garlic cloves. Surely I hadn’t lost finger strength that quickly? Turns out, it wasn’t me. It was the garlic. Since that first Australian head of garlic, I’ve discovered that Australian garlic is tighter than the US variety. Over there, a few gentle rubs prise the cloves apart. Here, you’ve really got to put some effort in – I suspect that’s why you can buy a packet of garlic cloves in supermarkets and I never saw such a product in the States. Garlic in Australia is more expensive, too. Continue reading...

Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times. articles.author: Nils Pratley
articles.content: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. Continue reading...

articles.content: The practice you’ve noticed is colloquially known as ‘review gating’, writes consumer affairs and policy professional Kat George . And no, it isn’t legal Read more Australian customer service questions I have noticed that when I get an email inviting me to review a product or service I have purchased online or physically, if I select a high rating I am taken to Google to write a review. However, if I select a low rating, I am then told “We are sorry” etc and asked what is wrong. I am not taken to Google to write a review. This would lead to very biased reviews. Is this practice legal? – Tom, Queensland Kat says: Screening reviews and sorting feedback based on a consumer’s initial sentiment is known colloquially online as “review gating” . It’s a dark pattern that is common enough that Google has banned it outright. And while the Australian consumer law doesn’t name the practice explicitly, it is clearly prohibited under laws relating to business reviews and false and misleading practices. Continue reading...
